chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sa'id ibn Yasar, who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'May I be your ransom,'

a woman handed over some wealth from her own wealth to her husband for him to work with, and said to him when she handed it over to him: 'Spend from it. If an event occurs with you [i.e., you die], whatever you have spent from it is permissible and good. If an event occurs with me [i.e., I die], whatever you have spent from it, then it is permissible and good.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'Repeat the question to me, O Sa'id.' So when I went to repeat the question to him, the owner of the matter intervened, and he was present with me, so he repeated to him (peace be upon him) similar to that.

When he finished, he (peace be upon him) pointed with his finger to the owner of the question and said: 'O you! If you know that she delegated that to you, between you and her and between Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, then it is permissible and good,' three times.

Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah, Majestic is His Name, says in His Book: "But if they of themselves be pleased to give up to you a portion of it, then eat it with enjoyment and with wholesome result."'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a wife giving her husband her personal wealth with a condition that he keeps what he spends regardless of who dies first?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) validates the wife’s stipulation that the husband’s spending from her capital remains lawful (halal) and pure (tayyib) regardless of who dies first, emphasizing the mutual trust between spouses. He confirms this by citing Surah An-Nisa 4:4, linking the specific condition of 'willingness' (nafs) to the Quranic concept of accepting gifts with a clear conscience. This ruling highlights the flexibility in marital financial arrangements within Shia jurisprudence, provided the transfer is consensual and free from dispute.
